sections.heading: Abstract
sections.where: Title page, White Paper v1.1, July 22, 2025
paragraphs: This white paper, dated July 22, 2025 and issued under Anza by Quentin Kniep, Jakub Sliwinski, and Roger Wattenhofer, describes Alpenglow, a consensus protocol aimed at worldwide high-throughput PoS chains. The title line pairs the protocol with a bandwidth-and-latency promise. Its voting piece, Votor, is said to finalize a block in one voting round when 80% of stake is participating, and in two voting rounds when only 60% of stake is responsive. The two modes run concurrently. After a block has been distributed, the paper states the finalization delay as the minimum of one network delay among an 80% stake set and two network delays among a 60% stake set.

The distribution piece, Rotor, is based on erasure coding. Participating nodes are said to supply bandwidth in proportion to stake, which is how the design tries to remove the leader bottleneck. The paper claims that total available bandwidth is then used asymptotically optimally. Resilience is labeled with the distinctive pattern "20+20": the protocol is claimed to tolerate harsh network conditions plus an adversary controlling 20% of stake, and a further 20% of stake may be offline when the network assumptions are stronger.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
paragraphs: The introduction retells a line often attributed to Thomas J. Watson, that the world market might hold about five computers, notes that the attribution is disputed, and mentions Howard H. Aiken among people tied to similar remarks. Moving a single word, the paper asks instead about five world computers. In this picture a world computer takes transactions as commands and updates an internal bookkeeping state, while giving users everywhere one shared environment. The machine is itself spread worldwide: dozens, hundreds, or thousands of processors joined by the internet. The claimed advantages over even an advanced traditional computer are survival of many component crashes, and resistance to any authority, including an evil botnet, that would corrupt the machine for other users. The paper gives blockchain as the current name for that machine, and then presents Alpenglow.

Rotor is described as an optimized, simplified variant of Solana's Turbine dissemination protocol. Turbine is credited with bringing erasure-coded information dispersal to permissionless blockchains. Because Rotor uses the bandwidth the nodes collectively provide, the paper claims asymptotically optimal throughput. Consensus designs that leave the leader's bandwidth as a bottleneck are said to suffer low throughput. Votor is said to inherit simplicity from the Simplex line of protocols and to carry that simplicity into proof of stake, so leaders can rotate without heavyweight view-change machinery. Ordinarily the paper claims finality after one voting round, while a conservative two-round procedure runs at the same time as backup.

sections.heading: 1.1 Alpenglow Overview
paragraphs: The overview starts from the participant set. Alpenglow runs on n nodes, and n can be in the thousands. The set is known and fixed for a stretch labeled an epoch. Every participant may message every other participant directly. Each node has a known cryptocurrency stake. The paper says that if one node holds twice the stake of another, it earns twice the fees and provides twice the outgoing bandwidth. Time is partitioned into slots. Each slot has a number and a designated leader, and each leader serves a fixed run of consecutive slots called the leader window. Before an epoch, a threshold verifiable random function fixes which node leads each slot.

A leader collects new transactions, directly from users or relayed by other nodes, and builds a block. The block is made of slices so that construction can be pipelined, and those slices break into shreds that give fault tolerance while spreading load evenly. Rotor, using erasure coding, spreads the shreds. The stated aim is stake-fair use of total outgoing bandwidth, avoiding a leader bottleneck. The leader continually sends shreds to relay nodes, and the relays forward them to the other nodes. Completion of one block is the cue for the following leader to begin its own block. Concurrently, every node eventually receives the new block. Incoming shreds and slices are stored in Blokstor.

Nodes next cast ballots saying whether they back the proposal. The overview defers vote types and aggregated certificates to the voting definitions, and the local record of those objects to Pool. Votor's rule, as summarized here, is that a correctly constructed block that arrives in time gets a supporting vote, while a late block gets a skip vote, because trust in the leader is absent or the network looks unstable. When stake above a super-majority threshold backs a proposal, that proposal finalizes at once. If something goes wrong, one more voting round decides whether to skip. A later subsection covers how a leader builds blocks and which parent it extends. Repair is how a node obtains missing shreds, slices, or blocks, including the contents of an earlier block that has become an ancestor of a finalized block.

The overview then points to the correctness arguments: safety when the network is unreliable, liveness when the network is reliable, and a further case with many crash failures. The following major section is described as useful for understanding Alpenglow without being required for the correctness claim. It is slated to cover a new Rotor relay sampling method, transaction execution, reconnection after lost contact, resynchronization after severe outages, and dynamic timeouts for a crisis. Parameter choices come next, followed by simulations on Solana's then-current node and stake distribution, one for bandwidth and one for latency. The remainder of the introduction is reserved for security goals, performance metrics, related work, the model, and cryptographic tools.

sections.heading: 1.2 Fault Tolerance
paragraphs: Safety and security are called the foremost aims of any consensus protocol. The paper recalls the usual goal of withstanding adversaries that control up to 33% of stake, the bound it also calls "3f + 1", and traces that result to Pease, Shostak, and Lamport in 1980, when the node counts they studied were small. It says today's blockchains have thousands of nodes, that the 33% bound still holds for large populations, and that attacking thousands of nodes is a different undertaking from attacking one or two. Running a thousand Byzantine nodes would in the paper's estimate, likely take billions of USD in staking capital, and punishable misbehavior would forfeit that capital. The paper therefore expects real large-scale faults to sit significantly below 33% Byzantine stake, and to come from misconfiguration, software bugs, and network or power outages: accidents rather than coordinated attacks.

That picture is the paper's reason to revisit the classic bound. Alpenglow rests on the "5f + 1" threshold from earlier fast-consensus literature. The paper says this bound is less tolerant of orthodox Byzantine attacks. Two voting rounds are required for finalization when the adversary is strong. When adversarial stake is smaller, or the adversary is not misbehaving continuously, the paper says a correct protocol in this family can still finish in one voting round. The safety and liveness sections are said to rely on Assumption 1: Byzantine nodes control less than 20% of stake, while everyone else—more than 80% of stake—behaves correctly.

Alpenglow is described as partially synchronous. Under Assumption 1, the paper claims that even an adversary who completely controls the network, inspecting, delaying, and scheduling communication among correct nodes at will cannot violate safety. An outage or partition is said to pause the protocol until communication returns, without an incorrect outcome. If the network is not under attack, or the adversary does not use a network advantage, the paper claims tolerance for a larger share of nodes that simply crash. Assumption 2, which a later section is said to distinguish from Assumption 1, states that Byzantine nodes control less than 20% of stake, other nodes holding up to 20% of stake may crash, and the remaining nodes, controlling more than 60% of stake, are correct.

sections.heading: 1.3 Performance Metrics
paragraphs: The paper claims Alpenglow reaches the fastest consensus the setting allows. Once a block is distributed, finalization time is again the minimum of one delay at 80% of stake and two delays at 60% of stake. The delay symbol is a network delay among a stake-weighted fraction of nodes, with the precise definition left to the model section. An 80% majority mechanism and a 60% majority mechanism run concurrently. A low-latency cluster holding 60% of stake is expected to finish sooner along the two-delay path, while more remote nodes may finish sooner along the single-delay path, so the protocol takes the minimum. Low latency is tied to usability: users get transaction finality sooner and see results with little delay.

Throughput is measured as transaction bytes per second or as transactions per second. On that metric the paper claims asymptotically optimal use of total available bandwidth. After those two results, it adds the aim of keeping protocol overhead small, including computation and other resource demands. Simplicity is treated as desirable even though it is hard to quantify. The paper says a simple protocol is easier to reason about easier to implement correctly, and more convenient to upgrade and optimize.

sections.heading: 1.4 Related Work
paragraphs: The paper limits this survey to each protocol as it was published, leaving aside techniques that could hypothetically be added later. On bandwidth, it groups PBFT, Tendermint, and HotStuff as leader protocols in which one node must deliver the proposed payload to every replica. That dissemination duty is called a defining limit on throughput. DAG protocols are presented as a line of work in which every node disseminates data. The paper says they pay a latency penalty. Some of them reduce that penalty by skipping a step the paper calls "certifying" the disseminated data. Mysticeti is the example: a leader block can be confirmed in two voting rounds, after the block is spread and two later block layers reference it, which the paper counts as three network delays.

Most data, namely every non-leader block, is ordered when a leader block that certifies it becomes final, so the paper says most throughput is confirmed only after five network delays. It notes that some researchers worry this technique hurts robustness.

Erasure coding is the other high-throughput technique surveyed here. The leader encodes the payload into smaller fragments, sends those fragments to different nodes, and those nodes help disseminate them, balancing bandwidth. The paper credits Solana with pioneering this approach in blockchains, and places Alpenglow in the same line. A recent comparison framework is cited for the indication that erasure-coding the payload, represented there by DispersedSimplex, achieves better latency than DAG protocols.

On latency, the paper reviews protocols that finish after one voting round, often called fast or one-step consensus. DGV and FaB Paxos are described with a parameterized population of 3f+2p+1 replicas, where p is at least 0 and counts replicas the fast path does not need. Those protocols are said to be able to terminate in two network delays under optimistic conditions. The paper reports that later work found liveness and safety problems in landmark papers of this area, that SBFT addressed the correctness issues, and that SBFT can still finish after one voting round. SBFT is described as optimized for linear message complexity and therefore higher latency. The 3f+2p+1 lower bound is said to apply only to a restricted class of protocol. Single-shot designs are cited that need merely 3f+2p*−1 replicas, with p* at least 1.

The paper adds a practical warning: one-step finalization can increase latency, because one round waits for n−p replicas, while two rounds among the more geographically concentrated n−f−p replicas can finish sooner. Banyan is credited with renewing interest in fast Byzantine consensus by running a one-round mechanism and a two-round mechanism in parallel, so the better latency is the one that wins.

Kudzu is called Alpenglow's "academic sibling" and is given a simpler theoretical model. The paper says both designs use erasure coding for high throughput and both run one-round and two-round finalization paths in parallel. The differences it lists begin with the trust model: Kudzu is permissioned, while Alpenglow is proof of stake. Voting weight is described as the usual consequence of that difference, whereas erasure-coded dissemination does not translate easily from one model to the other. Alpenglow uses leader windows in which the leader streams data without interruption, which the paper says improves throughput, and concurrent handling of slots lets block time be shorter than the latency bound. Fast leader handoff lets the next leader start a block as soon as it has the previous block.

With Assumption 3, the paper claims Alpenglow has higher resilience to crash faults than the sibling design. In Kudzu a node may vote upon the first fragment of a proposal; in Alpenglow a node votes after reconstructing a full proposal. The paper says the fragment rule is faster in theory, while the practical gap is only part of a single network delay. Alpenglow can set its erasure-coding expansion ratio freely. The paper suggests a ratio of 2, and says Kudzu needs a higher ratio. Hydrangea is presented as later work that parameterizes Byzantine and crash resilience in a related way. Its population is n = 3f+2c+k+1. Under partial synchrony it withstands f Byzantine faults together with c crash faults, and the count of nodes excused from one-round finalization is the floor of (c+k)/2.

The paper's Hydrangea example, for one-round termination among 80% of nodes, sets that unused count, the crash parameter, and k each to 20%, and sets f to 13%, for a total of 33% faulty nodes. Against that example it claims Alpenglow can tolerate f below 20% and a total of 40% faulty nodes, while needing Assumption 3 when the fault rate is higher than 20%. Hydrangea is said to leave the leader as a bandwidth choke point and in the authors' view, to remain underspecified for a practical implementation. The parameterization itself is called an interesting contribution that could also be applied to Alpenglow.

sections.heading: 1.5 Model and Preliminaries
paragraphs: Objects in the paper are written as a name plus parameters, meaning a deterministic encoding of that type and those parameters. An epoch is the interval between rejuvenations that allow the participant set to change, numbered 1, 2, 3, and so on. Participants register or unregister two epochs ahead: membership and weights for epoch e+1 are locked in when epoch e−1 finishes, early enough that everyone agrees on the set and the stake when epoch e+1 begins. The system has n nodes. Their jobs are to send and relay messages and to validate blocks, and the paper notes that such nodes are sometimes called validators. The set is static during an epoch and publicly known, including address, port, and public key.

That directory is announced and updated by a transaction on the chain, so every participant holds the same information. The paper says Solana then had about 1,500 nodes, that the protocol can in principle scale higher, and that bounding the population by some maximum may still be useful in practice.

Nodes exchange authenticated messages, and the protocol keeps every message under 1,500 bytes. Transport is authenticated UDP: either QUIC-UDP, or UDP with a pairwise message authentication code whose symmetric keys come from a public-key exchange. A broadcast is a loop over the other n−1 nodes. The paper says the network delay still dominates that loop. At 1 Gb/s, transmitting 1,500 shreds takes 18 ms, which it places well below an average network delay of about 80 ms. Reaching 80% of stake is said to require about 150 nodes and only about 2 ms, and voting messages are shorter. A multicast primitive from another network provider is left available, with DoubleZero and SCION named as examples.

Each node has a positive stake fraction, and the fractions sum to 1. Stake stays fixed during the epoch. Twice the stake means roughly twice the fees and twice the outgoing bandwidth. Every node still needs enough incoming bandwidth to receive blocks, and a minimum of outgoing bandwidth so it can distribute blocks when it is leader. Each node has a local clock, with 50 ppm offered as an example of reasonable accuracy. The analysis ignores drift, and the paper says drift can be absorbed into the timeout lengths. Clocks need not be synchronized, because a node uses only its own clock.

A slot is a natural number associated with a block. Nodes do not need to agree on when a slot starts or ends, although under ordinary network conditions the paper expects slots to become somewhat aligned. An epoch iterates slots from 1 through L. Solana's then-current epoch length of 432,000 slots is called possible, and a much shorter epoch, for example about 18,000 slots, is called advantageous when stake should change more quickly. The leader of each slot is given by a deterministic function known before the epoch starts. That leader serves a window of consecutive slots. A threshold verifiable random function is evaluated before the epoch and yields a public schedule.

Timeouts stop the protocol from waiting forever. For simplicity they are based on a global parameter, the maximum network delay between correct nodes during synchronous operation. The paper says the actual durations can still change with conditions, so correctness does not depend on the particular delay the network exhibits. In the writeup the delay bound is treated as a constant, with about 400 ms as the example. Timeouts measure short local intervals and do not assume a shared wall clock, so skew does not matter. The paper says even extreme drift can be folded in: to tolerate 5% clock drift, extend the timeouts by 5%. Because the protocol is partially synchronous, it claims that timing and clock errors cannot by themselves derail it.

Byzantine nodes may misbehave arbitrarily, drop messages, and collude. Signing inconsistent information is given as a provable offense. Sending a message late is given as behavior that might be only an extraordinary delay and therefore not punishable. Together, Byzantine nodes own strictly less than 20% of stake. Up to an additional 20% of stake may be crashed under the conditions discussed in the crash section. The remaining nodes are correct. The analysis treats the adversary as static over one epoch. The network is the partially synchronous setting with an unknown global stabilization time. Messages between correct nodes eventually arrive, but before that time they may take arbitrarily long. Safety is claimed for every delay pattern: correct nodes still emit one shared sequence of blocks.

Liveness is claimed only while the network is synchronous and messages among correct nodes arrive in time. After stabilization, a message sent at a given instant arrives no later than one maximum delay after the later of that instant and the stabilization time.

During synchrony the paper says the protocol rarely waits out a timeout. Actual message delay is modeled as a smaller, variable, unknown quantity used only for latency analysis. The paper classifies Alpenglow as optimistically responsive, so common-case performance depends on actual delay and not on the timeout bound. A delay written for a stake fraction is the time in which every member of some set holding at least that fraction of stake sends a message to every member of the set. If the nodes holding 60% of stake are geographically close, the paper says two delays at 60% can take less time than one delay at 80%.

The purpose of the chain is a sequence of finalized blocks such that every node outputs transactions in the same order. Every block has a parent, starting from a notional genesis block, and blocks that reach finality assemble into one parent-linked spine. Finalizing a block finalizes all of its ancestors. Ordering is by slot number, and a child must have a higher slot than its parent. For each slot, either a block produced by that slot's leader may be finalized, or the protocol may yield a skip. Blocks in finalized slots are delivered in order to the execution layer.

The paper's safety claim, attached to its first theorem, says that if a correct node finalizes block b in slot s, then any block that any correct node finalizes in a slot at or after s is a descendant of b. Its liveness claim, attached to the second theorem, says that across a long enough synchronous stretch, honest participants finalize fresh blocks that honest leaders produced.

sections.heading: 1.6 Cryptographic Techniques
paragraphs: The paper assumes a collision-resistant hash, with SHA-256 as the example, and unforgeable digital signatures. Every node knows every other node's public key. Signatures from different signers may be combined without interaction. Technically the paper requires only non-interactive multi-signatures, aggregation of signatures on one common message, and it names BLS as one way to build them. Aggregate signatures are what allow a certificate to fit in a short message, as long as the node count does not exceed the chosen maximum.

For integers Gamma at least gamma and gamma at least 1, a (Gamma, gamma) erasure code encodes an m-bit string as Gamma pieces. Each piece has length m/gamma plus a term logarithmic in Gamma, the extra bits being the index. Any gamma pieces reconstruct the string. The decoder also receives the length m, which the paper treats as constant by padding shorter payloads. A slice payload uses a Reed-Solomon code of this form. The expansion ratio is Gamma divided by gamma.

A Merkle tree commits to the vector of pieces. It is a full binary tree whose leaves are the piece hashes, each joined to a marker identifying that hash as a leaf. Each internal node is the hash of its two children, and the root is the commitment. The validation path for an index is the list of sibling hashes from that leaf up to the root. A checker recomputes the path and accepts the piece when the recomputed root equals the claimed root. Collision resistance is used to conclude that a different piece cannot have a valid proof for the same position in the same tree.

Encoding takes a payload, erasure-codes it, builds the Merkle tree, and returns the root together with each piece and its path. The root is uniquely associated with the payload. Decoding takes the root and a set of gamma pieces of the correct length, each with a valid path. It also checks that the root is the Merkle root of a full Gamma-piece encoding of some message, or it fails. On failure the paper claims that no gamma-piece subset tied to that root can be decoded, and that the root was maliciously constructed in a demonstrable way. The procedure reconstructs a candidate, re-encodes it, rebuilds the tree, and returns the candidate only when the new root matches. Otherwise it fails. That round trip is what gives the pass-or-fail property across every gamma-sized subset.

sections.heading: 2 The Alpenglow Protocol
paragraphs: The protocol section says it will specify Alpenglow in detail. A figure lays out the components and their interactions: Blokstor, Pool, and Votor on one side, and block creation, Rotor, Repair, and broadcast on the other. Arrows distinguish three kinds of information: shreds that carry block data, internal events, and votes or certificates. The subsections then define the data objects, dissemination, storage, votes, the local pool, the voting loop, leader production, repair, and the safety, liveness, and crash arguments.

sections.heading: 2.1 Shred, Slice, Block
paragraphs: A figure shows the data hierarchy as a double Merkle construction. Each slice has a Merkle root, and those roots are the leaves of a second tree whose root is the block hash. A shred is defined to fit in one UDP datagram. It carries the slot number, the slice index, the shred index, a bit flag, the slice root, the coded piece with its Merkle path, and a signature. The signature is the leader's signature on a slice object binding the slot, the slice index, the flag, and the root. A slice is the input to Rotor. Any gamma of the Gamma shreds decode it. The slice record holds the slot, the index, the flag, the root, the decoded payload, and the same leader signature. The flag marks the last slice of the slot.

A block, for voting and consensus, is the sequence of every slice of one slot. If there are k slices, the last flag is 1 and every earlier flag is 0. Block data are the concatenation of the slice payloads. Those data include the parent slot and the parent hash. The paper also imposes limits, including a bound on the number of bytes and a bound on execution time. The block hash is the root of a perfect binary tree whose leaf count is the least power of two that is at least the slice count. The first leaves are the slice roots, each concatenated with a leaf label, and the remaining leaves are empty. An ancestor is any block reached by parent links, including the block itself, and a descendant is the inverse relation.

sections.heading: 2.2 Rotor
paragraphs: Rotor is the dissemination protocol. The leader wants to broadcast a block with low latency, balanced bandwidth use, and resilience to transmission failures, and it streams the block rather than waiting until the whole block exists. Each slice is an independent Rotor round and is sent as soon as it is ready, which pipelines production and transmission. For a slice the leader generates Gamma Reed-Solomon shreds, then places a Merkle tree on those shred hashes and signs that root. Every shred carries its Merkle path plus the signed root, and holds as much data and metadata as one UDP datagram allows. Any gamma shreds reconstruct the slice. As a further validity check, the receiver then generates the missing shreds, up to Gamma minus gamma of them.

For each slice the leader sends every shred directly to a node chosen as that shred's relay. Relays are sampled afresh for every slice. The paper says the sampling method is new, improves resilience, and is specified in the sampling section. Each relay broadcasts its shred to every node that still needs it, meaning everyone except the leader and the relay, in decreasing order of stake. A minor optimization delivers the shred to the next leader first, slightly improving latency for the node that needs the block most urgently. Authenticity is checked per shred. On the opening shred of a slice, the receiver verifies the Merkle path together with the leader signature, then keeps the verified root. On later shreds it checks only the path against that stored root.

A latency figure fixes gamma at 32 and plots average and median Rotor latency for total shred counts of 64, 80, 96, and 320. The paper says the reference lines are average and median network latency, and that a high expansion ratio of 10, hence 320 shreds, comes close to the single-delay latency in its latency lemma. All of the paper's simulations use the Solana stake distribution of epoch 780. Network latency is inferred from public data, and computation and transmission delays are omitted.

Rotor is defined to be successful for a slot when that slot's leader is correct and at least gamma of the corresponding relays are correct. If so, the paper says every correct node receives the leader's block. A faulty leader can send no data, in which case Rotor fails immediately. The rest of the resilience discussion assumes a correct leader. The paper says Rotor is likely to succeed when coding shreds are over-provisioned by at least 67%. The resilience lemma assumes expansion strictly above 5/3 and says that as gamma tends to infinity, a slice is received correctly with probability 1.

The sketch samples relays by stake, takes each relay's failure probability as less than 40% from the fault-tolerance section, and computes an expected count of correct relays of at least 60% of Gamma. Because 60% of a quantity larger than 5/3 times gamma is larger than gamma, more than gamma shreds are expected. A Chernoff bound is invoked for the infinite-gamma claim that at least gamma shreds arrive correctly at every node.

Rotor latency is described as lying between one and two network delays, depending on optimistic or pessimistic parameter assumptions. The latency lemma says that if Rotor succeeds, network latency is at most two delays, that a high expansion ratio can reduce latency, and that in the extreme of infinitely many nodes and infinite expansion the latency can be brought down to one delay. The Solana-stake figure is cited as illustration. The sketch says a correct leader delivers each shred to its relay in one delay, and correct relays deliver onward in a second delay. With many extra relays, correct relays may sit geographically between the leader and a receiver. With infinitely many relays and what the paper calls natural stake-distribution assumptions, at least gamma correct relays lie on the direct path, add no overhead, and the two legs sum to one delay.

Because both the leader and the relays are sampled by stake, each node expects to transmit data in proportion to its stake, which the paper aligns with stake-proportional rewards. When outbound capacity scales with stake weight, that capacity can be saturated aside from overhead. The bandwidth lemma fixes a leader sending at a rate no higher than the average outgoing bandwidth across nodes, allows any stake-proportional bandwidth distribution, and claims that every correct node receives block data at the leader rate divided by the expansion ratio, in expectation. Up to that expansion ratio, the paper calls the rate optimal. The proof says a node is selected as a relay, in expectation, Gamma times its stake fraction, and that each such selection delivers the leader rate divided by Gamma, hence the node receives at its stake fraction times the leader rate.

That node must forward the data to n−2 others, so its expected send rate is its stake fraction times the leader rate times n−2. Its outgoing bandwidth is n times the average bandwidth times its stake fraction. Whenever the leader sends no faster than the average, the paper concludes the node has enough outgoing bandwidth. The useful rate cannot exceed the leader's send rate, because only the leader knows the data, and it cannot exceed the average bandwidth, because every node must receive the data and the nodes' total send capacity is n times the average. Apart from expansion, the paper calls the result optimal. It adds that attacks on Rotor can affect liveness only. Safety is assigned to the rest of the protocol, which is claimed to hold under asynchrony and to use Rotor only for dissemination.

sections.heading: 2.3 Blokstor
paragraphs: Blokstor keeps whichever block Rotor delivers first for a given slot. When a shred arrives, the node stores it only if that slot, slice, and shred index are not already present, the piece and path are valid for the slice root at that index, and the signature is the leader's signature on the corresponding slice object. When the first complete block for a slot is in hand, Blokstor emits a block event into the voting loop, carrying the slot, the block hash, and the parent hash. Besides that first block, repair can fetch some other block into the store. If a block is the finalized block of its slot, the store must collect and keep only that block for the slot. Otherwise, before a safe-to-notarize event is emitted for a block, that block has to be stored as well.

sections.heading: 2.4 Votes and Certificates
paragraphs: The voting section opens with the two successful endings and the skip. If a leader gathers votes from at least 80% of stake, the block is finalized immediately after one round by a fast-finalization certificate. A node that has seen notarization votes totaling 60% of stake then casts its second-round vote. Once a second-round tally covering 60% of stake backs the block, finalization follows as well. Stake that judges the block late can aggregate into a skip certificate, after which the proposal is dropped.

Five vote objects are defined, each carrying the voting node's signature. A notarization vote and a notar-fallback vote each name a block's slot and hash. A skip vote and a skip-fallback vote each name a slot. A finalization vote names a slot. Five certificate types aggregate votes by cumulative stake. A fast-finalization certificate needs notarization votes totaling at least 80%. A notarization certificate needs notarization votes totaling at least 60%. A notar-fallback certificate needs notarization or notar-fallback votes totaling at least 60%. A skip certificate needs skip or skip-fallback votes totaling at least 60%. A finalization certificate needs finalization votes totaling at least 60%.

sections.heading: 2.5 Pool
paragraphs: Every node keeps a Pool of the votes and certificates it has seen for every slot. For each slot and each other node, the pool stores the first notarization or skip vote received, up to three notar-fallback votes, the first skip-fallback vote, and the first finalization vote. A node's stake is counted only once per slot. When enough votes have arrived to meet a certificate threshold, the pool generates that certificate. A certificate that is newly added, whether received or locally constructed, is broadcast to all other nodes. One certificate of each type is stored for the corresponding block or slot. The paper notes that if a correct node generates a fast-finalization certificate, it has also generated the notarization certificate, and that certificate in turn implies the notar-fallback certificate.

There are two ways to finalize. A finalization certificate on a slot slow-finalizes the unique notarized block in that slot. A fast-finalization certificate on a block fast-finalizes that block. Whenever a block is finalized, by either path, its ancestors are finalized first. The pool emits a block-notarized event when it holds a notarization certificate. It emits parent-ready for a slot that is the first of its leader window once it already has either a notarization certificate or a notar-fallback certificate on some earlier block, plus skip certificates for every slot strictly between that block and the window start. The paper points to later lemmas for the claim that in every slot, every correct node casts exactly one notarization vote or skip vote, and only afterward may emit fallback events and cast additional votes.

The fallback events are gates on those additional votes. Safe-to-notarize for one block is the paper's signal that a different block cannot be fast-finalized in the slot, so a notar-fallback vote for this block is safe. Safe-to-skip is the signal that no block in the slot can be fast-finalized, so a skip-fallback vote is safe. The totals used are the stake of notarization votes on a given block and the stake of skip votes on the slot. Safe-to-notarize is issued only after this node has already voted in the slot and has not notarized this block, and only when notarization stake on the block is at least 40%, or when skip stake plus that notarization stake is at least 60% and the notarization stake is at least 20%.

If the slot is first in its leader window, the event is emitted at once. Otherwise repair retrieves the block so its parent can be identified, and the event waits until the pool also holds a notar-fallback certificate for that parent.

Safe-to-skip is issued only after this node has voted in the slot and has not skipped it. The numeric condition adds skip stake to the notarization stake of every block in the slot, then subtracts the largest single block's notarization stake, and requires the result to be at least 40%. These events are inputs to the voting loop.

sections.heading: 2.6 Votor
paragraphs: Voting exists to notarize and finalize blocks, and finalized blocks are the protocol's output: one chain of parent references. A life-cycle figure shows the common case as leader transmission, relay transmission, notarization votes, and finalization votes, with notarization, fast-finalization, and slow-finalization marked along that timeline. For every slot the paper claims there is either a skip certificate, or some notarized or notar-fallback block whose ancestors are also notarized. The thresholds are meant to keep a malicious leader from blocking the certificates that liveness needs. If many correct nodes notarize the same block, every other correct node casts a notar-fallback for it; otherwise every correct node broadcasts a skip-fallback. A node can finalize as soon as it sees enough notarization votes.

A lower participation threshold produces the notarization certificate, and that certificate is what leads the node to send a finalization vote. The paper states the resulting latency as one voting round among nodes holding 80% of stake, or two voting rounds among nodes holding 60%.

Nodes use local clocks and emit timeouts. The first parent-ready event for the opening slot of a window starts timers for every block in that window. Two delays parameterize them. One is the protocol block time. The other is the remaining possible delay, beyond the block time, between setting the timers and receiving a correctly disseminated block. As a conservative constant, the paper says that remaining delay can be set to one maximum-delay unit plus two more, a sum it describes as larger than the time for the leader to observe the certificates plus Rotor's slice-dissemination latency. For window start s and slot i in the window, the timeout is the local clock plus the remaining delay plus (i−s+1) times the block time. These instants are said to match the latest arrival of a correct leader's block when the network is synchronous.

The paper says they can be optimized by a finer delay estimate or to address particular faults, including crashes. Because parent-ready is emitted only for a window's first slot, the offset is at least one, and a timeout is never scheduled in the past.

Votor keeps per-slot state, initially empty, for the two algorithms that follow. A slot can permanently record parent-ready for a parent hash, the fact that a notarization or skip vote was cast, the hash that was notarized, the fact that a notarization certificate is held, a terminal mark meaning a finalization vote was cast and no further vote will be cast in the slot, and a bad-window mark. The bad-window mark is set when the node casts a skip vote, a skip-fallback vote, or a notar-fallback vote. Separately, each slot may have a pending block, initially empty. Pending blocks are retried for notarization when a condition that failed earlier may later hold.

The event loop is single-threaded. On a block event, the node tries to notarize. Success triggers a scan of pending blocks. If the slot is not yet voted, the block is saved as pending. On a timeout, if the slot is not yet voted, the node tries to skip the whole window. On a block-notarized event, the node records the certificate and tries to cast a finalization vote. On parent-ready, the node records the parent hash, scans pending blocks, and starts the timers for every slot in the window. On safe-to-notarize, the node first tries to skip the window and then if the terminal mark is absent, broadcasts a notar-fallback vote and marks the window bad. On safe-to-skip, it does the same with a skip-fallback vote.

The helpers carry out those steps. One function returns the slot numbers of the leader window that contains a given slot. The timeout setter schedules each of them at the clock formula above. Notarization does nothing if the slot is already voted. On the first slot of a window it requires that parent-ready holds the parent hash. On any later slot it requires that the previous slot records a notarization vote for the parent hash. When the condition holds the node broadcasts a notarization vote, records the voted mark and the notarized hash, clears the pending block, tries finalization immediately, and reports success. Finalization broadcasts a finalization vote and sets the terminal mark only when three conditions hold together: the notarization certificate for that hash is recorded, the node itself notarized that hash, and the window is not marked bad.

The window-skip helper walks every slot of the window. For each slot that is not yet voted, it broadcasts a skip vote, records the voted mark and the bad-window mark, and clears the pending block so a later notarization will not be cast. The pending-block scan walks slots in increasing order and retries notarization on each stored block. Together, the loop and the helpers are the paper's full statement of when a correct node notarizes, skips, falls back, or sends the second-round finalization vote.

sections.heading: 2.7 Block Creation
paragraphs: The leader of a window produces a block for every slot in the window. After parent-ready names a parent, the paper says a first-slot block with that parent will be valid: other nodes receive the same certificates, emit the same event, and all correct nodes vote for the block. In the common case only one parent-ready event is emitted, and the leader must build on that parent. If several parent-ready events name different blocks, which the paper attributes to a misbehaving previous leader or to network delay, the leader may choose any of them. An optimization lets the leader start building before any parent-ready event. Usually the previous slot's block arrives first and its certificate arrives one network delay later. Starting early avoids that extra wait in the common case.

If the leader began with one parent and the only ready parent is different, it may name the new parent in the contents of some later slice. Slices before that slice are ignored for execution. The paper allows the indicated parent to change only once, and only in the first slot of a window.

Once some parent-ready event has been observed, the leader produces the rest of the window without inserted delays. The first block extends a parent for which parent-ready was emitted, the next block extends that first block, and each later block extends its predecessor. A handover figure shows the new leader emitting the first slice of its first block as soon as it has the last slice of the previous leader. The lower panel shows the same handover when the leader switches parents. The construction algorithm waits until the previous slot's block has arrived or parent-ready is set, generates the first block, and streams slices through Rotor while parent-ready is still absent.

If the ready parent is not the one already in use, it picks any ready parent and regenerates the block from the current slice index. It then streams further slices until one block time has passed on the local clock. For each remaining slot it generates a block whose parent is the block just produced and runs Rotor across one block time.

sections.heading: 2.8 Repair
paragraphs: Repair retrieves a block of a given hash that Blokstor does not hold. It is triggered once the pool has a certificate of signatures on a notarization or notar-fallback object for that slot and hash. Four functions support the fetch. Sampling chooses a node at random by stake. A slice-count query returns the number of slices, the hash sitting at that last position, and the Merkle path of that hash under the block hash. The caller checks that this hash is the last non-empty leaf and that the hashes to its right correspond to empty subtrees. A slice-hash query returns one slice root and its path under the block hash. A shred query returns one shred for a slot, slice index, shred index, and slice root. Any of these calls can fail verification and return empty, for example when the answer is invalid or the contacted node does not have the data.

The repair algorithm starts with an unknown slice count and repeats a stake-sampled slice-count query until the answer verifies. It then handles every slice concurrently. For each slice it repeats a stake-sampled slice-hash query until the root verifies, and for each shred index it repeats a stake-sampled shred query until a valid shred is stored. The paper presents this loop as the way a node fills in a certified block, including an ancestor it missed.

sections.heading: 2.9 Safety
paragraphs: In the safety argument, a certificate counts as existing when a correct node has observed it, and an ancestor counts as existing when parent links under the given hashes reach that block. The first lemma says a correct node casts only one notarization vote or one skip vote in a slot, exclusively. Both vote types are cast only from the notarization helper and the window-skip helper, both helpers vote only when the voted mark is absent, and both set that mark, so the vote cannot be repeated.

The fast-finalization property says that a fast-finalized block excludes three things in its slot: notarization of any other block, notar-fallback certification of any other block, and a skip certificate. The argument takes a correct node that fast-finalized the block, which means notarization votes cover at least 80% of stake. Byzantine stake is less than 20%, so a set of correct nodes holding more than 60% notarized it. That set cannot skip or notarize a different block, and the paper concludes that notarization stake on any other block is smaller than 40%. Correct nodes cast notar-fallback votes only on safe-to-notarize. For a different block, the paper's proof invokes either at least 40% notarizing that block, or at least 60% notarizing it or skipping the slot.

Only stake outside the correct set, less than 40%, can do either, so no correct node notar-fallbacks the other block. Skip-fallback likewise needs at least 40% skipping or notarizing a different block, which that outside stake cannot supply, and the correct set itself does not skip or skip-fallback.

A correct node that casts a finalization vote in a slot does not cast a notar-fallback or a skip-fallback there. Finalization adds the terminal mark, and both fallback broadcasts require that mark to be absent. A fallback vote adds the bad-window mark, and finalization requires that mark to be absent, so the opposite order is blocked as well. If correct nodes holding more than 40% notarize one block, no other block in the slot can be notarized. A notarization certificate requires 60% of stake, so some node in that correct set would have had to notarize both blocks, contradicting the one-vote lemma. The slot therefore admits only one notarized block: notarization already implies, with Byzantine stake below 20%, that correct nodes above 40% notarized that block.

If a correct node finalizes a block, the block is also notarized. On the fast path at least 80% of stake notarized it. Byzantine stake below 20% means correct nodes holding more than 60% broadcast notarization votes, and correct nodes observe a notarization certificate. On the slow path, finalization ballots covering at least 60% of stake appear, including some correct nodes. A correct node casts that vote only after observing a notarization certificate, and the uniqueness lemma forces the certificate to be for the same block. The slow-finalization property repeats the three exclusions. At least 60% cast finalization votes, so correct nodes holding more than 40% did so.

Those nodes observed one common notarization certificate, had themselves notarized that block, and by the one-vote and no-fallback lemmas, cast no other vote in the slot. They hold more than 40%, and every certificate needs at least 60%, so the paper says no skip certificate and no certificate on another block can be produced.

If a notarization or notar-fallback certificate exists for a block, some correct node cast a notarization vote for it. Otherwise, with Byzantine stake below 20%, every correct node would see less than 20% notarizing the block. Both branches of safe-to-notarize require observing 20% notarizing it, so no correct node would emit the event, and that event is the only trigger for a notar-fallback vote. A certificate that needs at least 60% of stake on notarization or notar-fallback votes would then be impossible. Inside one leader window, a correct notarization vote implies that the same node notarized the ancestor in every earlier slot of the window. The first slot has no earlier window slot to check. A later notarization is allowed only when the previous slot records a notarization of the parent hash, and that record is written only by casting the notarization vote.

If a correct node notar-fallbacks a block that is not first in its window, then for the parent either some correct node notar-fallbacks the parent, or correct nodes holding more than 40% notarize the parent. Safe-to-notarize in that position requires a notarization or notar-fallback certificate on the parent, hence at least 60% of stake voted one of those ways. Byzantine stake below 20% leaves one of the two correct-node conclusions. The paper then lifts the claim to a whole window. If a block is notarized or notar-fallback certified, every earlier slot of its window contains an ancestor, and for each such ancestor either correct nodes above 40% notarized it or some correct node notar-fallback voted it. The proof uses the existence of a correct notarization vote, the ancestor chain inside the window, and induction through the parent step.

If some correct node finalizes a block, and another block in the same leader window has an equal or later slot and is notarized or notar-fallback certified for any correct observer, the later block is a descendant. The exclusion properties rule out two finalized-or-certified blocks in one slot, so the second slot is strictly later and is not the window's first slot. Some correct node notarized the later block and therefore notarized an ancestor in the slot just after the finalized block. If the later block does not descend from the finalized one, that ancestor's parent in the finalized slot is a different block. A correct notar-fallback on the ancestor would mean that other parent is notarized or notar-fallback certified, contradicting an exclusion property. Correct nodes above 40% notarizing the ancestor would also have notarized that other parent, contradicting the 40% uniqueness lemma.

The cross-window lemma takes a finalized block and a later-slot block in a different window that is notarized or notar-fallback certified, and concludes the later block is a descendant. The proof picks the highest ancestor of the later block that is still at or after the finalized slot and is itself notarized or notar-fallback certified. If that ancestor shares the finalized block's window, the previous lemma applies. Otherwise some correct node notarized the first block of the ancestor's window, which required parent-ready on its parent, so the parent is notarized or notar-fallback certified. A parent slot before the finalized slot would mean a skip certificate on the finalized slot. A parent in the finalized slot would be a second certified block there. A parent after the finalized slot would contradict the choice of the highest such ancestor.

The safety theorem then says that whenever an honest node finalizes block b at slot s, any block that any honest node later finalizes in a slot ≥ s must descend from b. The paper's proof cites notarization-from-finalization and the two chain lemmas.

sections.heading: 2.10 Liveness
paragraphs: If a correct node emits parent-ready for a window's first slot, it emits a timeout for every slot of that window, because the handler schedules them. Conversely, a timeout on a slot means the node emitted parent-ready for the first slot of that slot's window. If every correct node sets the timeout for a slot, every correct node casts a notarization vote or a skip vote there. The timeout handler calls the window-skip helper unless the voted mark is already set, and that mark is added only when one of those two votes is cast. If no set of correct nodes holding more than 40% notarizes the same block, no correct node adds the terminal finalization mark. That mark is added only after a notarization certificate, the certificate needs 60% notarizing one block, and Byzantine stake below 20% would then require correct stake above 40% on that block.

If every correct node times out a slot, then either every correct node eventually observes a skip certificate, or correct nodes holding more than 40% notarize one common block. The argument assumes the second alternative fails. All correct nodes vote, so each observes notarization or skip votes from a correct set holding at least 80% of stake under Assumption 1. For a node in that set, skip stake plus all notarization stake equals 80% plus any additional stake outside the set whose vote it has seen. The largest notarization total is at most 40% plus that outside stake. Subtracting leaves at least 40%, which meets safe-to-skip. A node that has not yet skipped emits that event, finds the terminal mark absent, and casts a skip-fallback vote. Every correct node therefore casts a skip or a skip-fallback, and all of them observe a skip certificate.

If correct nodes holding more than 40% notarize a block, every correct node eventually observes a notar-fallback certificate for it. The paper inducts on the distance from the first slot of the window. On the first slot, a correct node that refused both votes would still see more than 40% notarizing the block and would emit safe-to-notarize. It cannot hold the terminal mark, because that mark requires a notarization vote on a notarized block, no other block in the slot can be notarized, and this node did not notarize this one. It would therefore cast the notar-fallback, a contradiction. Every correct node votes one of the two ways, and the certificate is observed.

Off the first slot, the same reluctant node retrieves the block and identifies the parent. The correct nodes that notarized the block also notarized the parent in the previous slot. The induction hypothesis supplies a notar-fallback certificate for the parent, safe-to-notarize fires, and the same contradiction forces the fallback vote.

If every correct node times out a window, then for every slot in it every correct node observes either a notar-fallback certificate or a skip certificate. A slot without a skip certificate has, by the previous alternative, a block that correct nodes above 40% notarized, and that block then has a notar-fallback certificate. The same timeout assumption implies that every correct node emits parent-ready for the first slot of the next window. If skip certificates cover the whole window, the node already had parent-ready on some earlier block with skip certificates filling every slot up to this window, and the new skips extend the gap through the window. Otherwise the highest slot in the window without a skip certificate has a notar-fallback certificate, and skips fill every slot from that block to the next window. By induction, every correct node sets the timeout for every slot.

After stabilization, if the first correct node sets the window-start timeout at time t, every correct node emits parent-ready for that start and sets the window timeouts by t plus one maximum delay, because the justifying certificates are broadcast and arrive within that delay.

The liveness theorem takes a correct leader of a window starting at slot s. It assumes that no correct node set the window's timeouts before stabilization, and that Rotor succeeds for every slot of the window. It claims that every correct node finalizes the blocks that leader produces in every slot of the window. The paper's outline has four moves: bound the time at which correct nodes hold the blocks; show that a skip by one correct node would cover every later slot of the window; reduce the first such skip to a timeout rather than a fallback event; and show that this timeout arrives only after that node has already notarized the slot.

Every correct node sets the start-slot timeout. Let t be the first time a correct node does so; t is at or after stabilization. Within one further maximum delay the leader has recorded parent-ready and by the block-creation conditions, has reached the step where a parent is fixed. The leader finishes transmitting the block of a window slot k by t plus one maximum delay plus (k−s+1) block times. With Rotor successful, correct nodes receive that block by t plus three maximum delays plus the same block-time offset. Suppose some correct node fails to notarize one of these blocks, and take the earliest such slot. The correct leader produced the only valid block there, so the node skips it. The parent condition for later slots then prevents notarization anywhere later in the window, so the node skips every later slot as well.

Skip votes are cast by the window-skip helper, which runs after safe-to-notarize, safe-to-skip, or timeout. For this node's first skip in the window, safe-to-notarize cannot be the cause in an earlier slot, because every correct node notarized there, and at the skipped slot or later the event would require a skip that had already been cast. Safe-to-skip is ruled out the same way. A timeout has no effect on a slot the node already notarized, and the node cannot notarize a slot after that slot's timeout, so the triggering slot is at least the first skipped slot. Timeouts are scheduled later for higher slots, so the timeout of the first skipped slot is the earliest possible moment of the first skip. That moment is at least t plus the remaining timeout plus the block-time offset. With the remaining timeout equal to three maximum delays, it is at least t plus three maximum delays plus the offset.

By that same moment the node has received every block from the window start through the skipped slot. It has also emitted parent-ready for the window parent. The notarization condition therefore holds for the first block, and the pending-block scans, which run on both block arrival and parent-ready, cause notarization of every block up through the supposed skip, whatever the arrival order. That contradicts the choice of a node that skipped. The paper concludes that every correct node notarizes every block of the window, observes the fast-finalization certificate for each of them, and finalizes them.

sections.heading: 2.11 Higher Crash Resilience
paragraphs: This section sketches correctness when the network is less adversarial and crash faults are more numerous. The paper says that under harsh network conditions an adversary with over 20% of stake can attack Alpenglow, and that such an attack requires careful orchestration. It treats accidental errors, crashes, and DoS campaigns—functionally akin to crashes—as the failures that have historically caused more trouble for blockchains. The rest of the section uses Assumption 2 in place of Assumption 1, and adds Assumption 3 to express the attacker's weaker control of the network. Assumption 3, labeled Rotor non-equivocation, says that if one correct node receives a full block through Rotor, every other correct node that reconstructs a full Rotor block in that slot reconstructs this same block.

Crashed nodes are treated as equivalent to nodes with indefinite delay. Because the safety section argued safety under arbitrarily large delays, the paper claims safety still holds under Assumption 2. Liveness changes where the argument says correct nodes will see enough votes to trigger safe-to-notarize or safe-to-skip. With the added claim that two correct nodes cannot reconstruct different blocks in one slot, the paper says one of those two events must be emitted by every correct node after the correct nodes' votes are observed. If correct nodes holding at least 20% notarized a block, then skip stake plus that block's notarization stake is at least 60% and the notarization stake is at least 20%. Otherwise, skip stake plus all notarization stake minus the largest notarization total is at least the skip stake, which is at least 40%. A corollary says the liveness theorem holds under Assumptions 2 and 3 in place of Assumption 1.

If the leader is correct or crashed, the paper says Assumption 3 is never violated, because that leader produces at most one block per slot. The paper therefore claims that crashes alone, below 40% of stake, are always tolerated. The section then sketches a violation: an adversary distributes different blocks to different parties, and if many nodes have also crashed, correct nodes might not see enough votes to emit either fallback event, so the protocol could get stuck. A malicious leader might try to deliver two blocks so that one honest cohort rebuilds and backs the first while another rebuilds and backs the second. A correct node that receives two shreds for the same slice index with different Merkle roots, before it can reconstruct, will not vote. Network topology and the sampling of Rotor relays determine whether the split is feasible.

The paper's example uses two clusters of correct nodes whose internal latency is negligible beside the latency between the clusters. Stake in the example splits as 31% in each cluster, 18% adversarial, and 20% crashed. Relays in one cluster receive shreds of one block from the malicious leader, and relays in the other cluster receive shreds of a different block. Adversarial relays forward each block's shreds only toward its own cluster. Because of the inter-cluster delay, each cluster reconstructs its block before seeing any shred of the other, and Assumption 3 fails. The paper says that when nodes are distributed uniformly, it is harder to arrange for a large group to collect enough shreds of one slice before any shred of the matching slice of the other block.

sections.heading: 3 Beyond Consensus
paragraphs: The closing section discusses matters that sit outside the core consensus argument but still matter for understanding the protocol. The opening lists three nearby topics, sampling, rewards, and execution, then advanced failure handling, and finally the bandwidth and latency measurements. The numbered subsections that actually follow are sampling, voting versus execution, asynchrony in practice, dynamic timeouts, protocol parameters, bandwidth, and latency. Rewards do not receive a separate procedure in this file; stake-proportional fees were stated earlier as part of what stake means.

sections.heading: 3.1 Smart Sampling
paragraphs: To improve Rotor's resilience in practice, the paper specifies a committee sampler inspired by an earlier FA1 construction and intended to improve on FA1 with independent draws by reducing variance further. A partitioning of relative stakes into k bins is an assignment in which every node's stake is fully assigned and every bin sums to 1/k. Any procedure that produces such an assignment is a partitioning algorithm. Partition sampling, called PS-P, is instantiated with one partitioner and draws one set of Gamma samples in three steps. Each node whose stake exceeds 1/Gamma fills a number of bins equal to the integer part of its stake times Gamma, and only a remainder strictly below 1/Gamma stays eligible; every smaller node keeps its original stake. The partitioner then assigns those remainders into the bins that are left, a count equal to Gamma minus the integer placements. Each bin contributes one sample, drawn proportional to stake inside the bin.

One simple partitioner orders the nodes at random and cuts the sequence exactly every 1/k of relative stake. The paper says PS-P with that partitioner is already better than the published sampler it compares against, and that the topic deserves more research. For the formal comparison, the adversary may spread its stake across many nodes. The paper assumes that aggregate adversarial stake is below gamma/Gamma, equates that ratio with 1/kappa, and writes that gamma is then below the adversary's stake times Gamma. A lemma adds the restriction that every individual stake is below 1/Gamma. For any partitioner, the chance the adversary is sampled at least gamma times under PS-P is at most the chance under stake-weighted independent sampling. The count of adversarial samples is a Poisson binomial: Gamma independent Bernoulli trials whose success probabilities are the adversary's share of each bin.

Packing the adversary evenly in every bin makes the count binomial at the adversary's stake fraction, the same law as independent stake-weighted sampling. The paper cites that binomial law as the maximum-variance Poisson binomial, and therefore as the case that maximizes the chance of at least gamma successes when gamma is below Gamma.

A theorem removes the per-node size restriction and says that for any stake distribution, drawing at least gamma samples under PS-P is no more probable than under FA1 with independent fallback sampling. The reason given is that the integer-bin step is FA1, with this scheme as the fallback on the residual stake, so the lemma applies to the remainder. The paper then compares the sampler, using fully randomized partitioning, with FA1 independent sampling, ordinary stake-weighted sampling, and Turbine, on the current Solana stake distribution. A figure shows the probability that Rotor is unsuccessful under crash failures. Success for a block requires success on every slice, and the figure assumes 64 slices per block.

One panel uses 32 data shreds and 64 total shreds, with crashed stake marked at 40%, 30%, and 20%. The other uses 40% crashes and an expansion ratio of 2, with total shred counts of 64, 128, and 256. The surrounding text does not state numerical failure probabilities for the curves.

sections.heading: 3.2 Voting vs. Execution
paragraphs: The consensus sections omitted execution of blocks and of the transactions inside them. The paper says Solana, as of the writing, uses the synchronous model it calls eager execution. Leaders run the block prior to transmission, and every node runs it prior to casting a vote. Slices are pipelined, so the next slice can propagate while the previous slice executes. The paper says this can still add time on the critical path, because the last slice must be executed before a notarization vote can be sent.

Lazy, or asynchronous, execution lets nodes vote before executing. The paper says Compute Units then have to reflect actual execution cost, so the unit bounds on transactions and on the whole block keep execution timely. If the units are unrealistically optimistic, it says execution delay may grow without a bound. Distributed execution is described as related ongoing research. Validators use several machines, placed together to keep latency small. The paper says the aim, relative to a single machine, is higher transaction throughput, and elasticity: a node can meet a surge in traffic without permanently over-provisioning. Pilotfish and Stingray are named as examples of that line of work.

sections.heading: 3.3 Asynchrony in Practice
paragraphs: The model assumed that delayed messages are eventually delivered. The paper notes that in reality, and in the original formulation of partial synchrony, messages can be lost. Because arbitrary delay is already allowed, it says the protocol remains safe if messages are dropped. Two mechanisms are then described to restore liveness when the protocol makes no progress. A node that reboots or joins, and that has seen block b become final in slot s, does not need votes or certificates from earlier slots. By the safety theorem, any block that might be finalized in a later slot descends from b, and if any correct node emits parent-ready for a block, that block also descends from b.

The joining node needs a fast-finalization certificate for b, or a finalization certificate for the slot together with a notarization certificate for b. Repair retrieves b, then the parent can be identified and retrieved, and so on. A practical implementation might fetch missing blocks for many slots in parallel before verifying and repairing the ancestors.

Liveness after stabilization still depends on eventual delivery. Once a correct node has observed a finalization in a slot, votes and certificates from earlier slots are not needed for liveness. A lack of liveness is detected by a period in which no new slot is finalized. After a parameterized standstill, with about 10 seconds offered as the example during which the highest finalized slot stays unchanged, correct nodes start a retransmission routine. Each node broadcasts a finalization certificate for the highest slot it has observed: either a fast-finalization certificate covering some block, or else a slot finalization certificate paired with that block's notarization certificate. For every higher slot, nodes also broadcast certificates they have observed and the votes they themselves cast.

sections.heading: 3.4 Dynamic Timeouts
paragraphs: The paper says epochs depart from pure partial synchrony. Epoch changes work only if finality occurs at least once inside every epoch. When a block becomes final during epoch e, that shows epoch e−1 closed on an agreed state, which is what lets epoch e+1 begin with agreement on the nodes and their stake. The remedy is to extend timeouts when the situation looks dire. If a node has no finalized block across about 10 seconds of consecutive leader windows, the same standstill scale, it begins extending its timeouts by about 5% in every leader window. Nodes do not coordinate these extensions. As soon as finalized blocks appear again, they return immediately to the timeouts specified with the voting loop, again with no agreement required.

The paper says some nodes may still be using longer timeouts without jeopardizing correctness. Growth of about 5% per window is exponential, and the paper says the timeouts then become longer than the delay of a network or power disaster, so a finalized slot in each epoch can be guaranteed.

sections.heading: 3.5 Protocol Parameters
paragraphs: The parameter section collects values used in the paper's preliminary simulations and says testing is still needed before they are final. Some parameters are implicit and differ by epoch, especially the node count. The exposition uses about 1,500 nodes, and the paper says the count at the time of writing was closer to about 1,300. The simulation table sets 4 blocks per leader window, 32 data shreds per slice, 64 coding shreds per slice, a timeout increase of 5%, a maximum of 2,000 nodes, a standstill trigger of 10 seconds, a block time of 400 ms, and an epoch length of 18,000 slots.

sections.heading: 3.6 Bandwidth
paragraphs: The bandwidth section estimates Votor message sizes for a network of 1,500 nodes. The table's fields are a 96-byte BLS signature, an 8-byte slot, a 32-byte block hash where the message names a block, a 188-byte node bitmap on certificates, a 32-byte authentication field, and a 28-byte header. The stated totals are 196 bytes for a notarization vote, 384 for a notarization certificate, 384 for a fast-finalization certificate, 164 for a finalization vote, 352 for a finalization certificate, 164 for a skip vote, and 352 for a skip certificate. To save bandwidth, a node broadcasts just whichever finalization certificate it sees first.

Ordinarily, each node sends, once per slot, its notarization vote, its finalization vote, the notarization certificate, and a single finalization certificate. Accounting for the larger finalization certificate, the fast-finalization certificate, the paper says a node sends the sum of 196, 384, 384, and 164 bytes, multiplied by 1,500, on every 400 ms slot, and states the resulting rate as 32.27 Mbit/s.

Outgoing bandwidth is plotted for a consistent goodput of 500 Mbps. The caption says that goodput is the case in which the leader role sends at 1 Gbps when the expansion ratio is 2. Rotor and Votor are shown separately against validators ordered from small to large. The text does not tabulate a per-validator bandwidth beyond that figure.

sections.heading: 3.7 Latency
paragraphs: The latency section reports a simulation of Alpenglow in what the paper calls a realistic environment. Stake mirrors Solana's weights as of writing (epoch 780), and inter-node latencies come from real-world measurements. Some delays are excluded, in particular block execution time, and the paper says a different stake distribution would change the results. One histogram fixes the block leader in Zurich, described as the authors' location then. Relays are chosen at random according to stake, and each bar averages 100,000 simulated executions. The plot shows latency to successive stages against the fraction of stake that has reached the stage.

Network latency is one series: with the then-current Solana distribution, about 65% of stake is within 50 ms round-trip of Zurich, and a long tail has more than 200 ms of network latency from Zurich. The paper treats that series as a lower bound, with the example that a node 100 ms from Zurich needs at least 100 ms for any protocol to finalize a block there.

The next series is Rotor, the time at which nodes have received gamma shreds and can reconstruct a slice. Another series marks the time at which a node has notarization votes from at least 60% of stake. The final series is finalization time. A node may finalize by constructing a fast-finalization certificate from 80% of the original notarization stake, by constructing a finalization certificate from 60% of the finalization votes, or by receiving one of those certificates from a third party, whichever comes first. For the fixed Zurich leader, the paper reports that even the slowest node finalizes in under 270 ms, while a median node finishes nearly as soon as the quickest nodes, at roughly 115 ms.

A second histogram chooses the leader at random according to stake. The paper says Zurich is more central than an average leader, so the numbers are somewhat higher than in the fixed-leader plot, with median finalization near 150 ms. A short thanks names people who gave input; that list is acknowledgment, not a protocol result. The bibliography was not treated as findings.
